# Regular Expressions: Languages and Filters

## Regular Expressions as String Filters

Goals:

* Use a regex as a filter: keep the rows where _some part_ of a string fits.

* Tell a filter from a language: `str.contains` vs. `str.fullmatch`.

* Build boolean masks with `str.contains`, and combine them with `&`, `|`, `~`.

::: notes
Bridge from sets: a subset is just a predicate. Regex gives us predicates on strings.
:::

## From Sets to Strings {.smaller}

Sets: $A=\{x\in U: P(x)\}$

\

A regular expression $r$ does two different jobs.

* **Language.** $L(r)=\{w\in\Sigma^*: \text{the whole of } w \text{ matches } r\}$.
  A set of _strings_, usually infinite.
  In Python: `re.fullmatch(r, w)`. In pandas: `df['col'].str.fullmatch(r)`.

* **Filter.** Keep the rows whose string has _some part_ that matches $r$.
  A set of _rows_, a subset of the dataframe.
  In pandas: `df['col'].str.contains(r)`.

\

Today: languages first, then filters.

## Regex vs. Language {.smaller}

Fix an alphabet of characters, $\Sigma$.

Then a pattern $r$ denotes the language $L(r)=\{w\in\Sigma^*: \text{the whole of } w \text{ matches } r\}$

* if no string matches the pattern,  $L=\varnothing$

* the empty pattern matches only the empty string ⇒ $L=\{\varepsilon\}$

* pattern `a` means $L=\{$`a`$\}$

* Concatenated patterns `AB` means $L(A)L(B)=\{xy:x\in L(A),y\in L(B)\}$

* Union of patterns: `A|B` means $L(A)\cup L(B)$

* Kleene Star: `A*` means all finite concatenations from $L(A)$ (incl. $\varepsilon$)

::: notes
Same spirit as set algebra: union / product / closure.
No anchors here: a language always means the whole string.
:::

## Say the Set 

\ 

`(ab|ba)*`: strings over `{a,b}` that are concatenations of `ab` or `ba`.

\

`(0|1)*11(0|1)*`: all binary strings containing 11 as a substring.

\

`1(01|10)*0`: binary strings that start with 1, end with 0, and are filled with `{0,1}` pairs that flip from `1` to `0` or vice versa.

## Same Pattern, Two Jobs {.smaller}

`pattern = 'Latte'`, so $L($`pattern`$)=\{$`Latte`$\}$. How many café orders does each line keep? Predict, then run.

A **Filter** card in Pattern Eights was `contains`.

```{pyodide}
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/UBC-CS/dsci220/refs/heads/main/data/cafe_orders.csv')

pattern = 'Latte'
print(df['drink'].str.fullmatch(pattern).sum())   # whole string is in L
print(df['drink'].str.match(pattern).sum())       # string starts with something in L
print(df['drink'].str.contains(pattern).sum())    # some part of the string is in L
```

::: notes
fullmatch is membership in L: only Latte itself. contains is a filter: it also
keeps Iced Latte, Chai Latte, Matcha Latte. Those strings are not in L; they
are in Sigma* L Sigma*, the strings with a part in L. Anchors turn a filter
back into membership: contains('^Latte$') keeps the same rows as
fullmatch('Latte').
Counts: 2, 2, 5. Try pattern = 'Iced' too: 0, 2, 2.
The DS2200 callback from the warm-up: not in L, but contains keeps it.
:::


## Back to the Cafe

Suppose a column `drink` has values like:
<span class="rule">"Iced Latte", "Drip Coffee", "Americano", "Chai Latte", "Tea", "Espresso"</span>

\ 

Goals:

1. Keep espresso-style drinks: "espresso", "americano", "latte", or "cappuccino"

2. "Iced" appears as a whole word

3. Drinks that end with “Tea”

## Typical Patterns


Whole word: <span class="rule">r'\\biced\\b'</span>

Starts with: <span class="rule">r'^Iced'</span>

Ends with: <span class="rule">r'Tea$'</span>

Optional word: <span class="rule">r'^(Iced )?Latte$'</span>

One of set (case-insensitive):  

<center>
<span class="rule"> r'(?i)\\b(espresso|americano|latte|cappuccino)\\b'</span>
</center>

## Cafe continued

```{pyodide}
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/UBC-CS/dsci220/refs/heads/main/data/cafe_orders.csv')

# regex
esprestr = r'(?i)\b(espresso|americano|latte|cappuccino)\b'
icedrestr = r'(?i)\biced\b'
tearestr = r'(?i)tea$'

# masks
espressoish = df['drink'].str.contains(esprestr, regex=True, na=False)
iced       = df['drink'].str.contains(icedrestr, regex=True, na=False)
teas       = df['drink'].str.contains(tearestr,  regex=True, na=False)

# Set algebra on masks:
E_or_I   = espressoish | iced          # union
I_and_T  = iced & teas                 # intersection
not_I    = ~iced                       # complement

# Project the data:
subset = df[E_or_I]
subset
```

## Reminder: From Filter to Language {.smaller}

Let $\Sigma$ = letters, numbers, and spaces.

Pattern <span class="rule">(?i)(espresso|americano|latte|cappuccino)</span> denotes a language $L\subseteq \Sigma^*$.

This parallels:

Set: $L=\{\,w\in\Sigma^*: \text{the whole of } w \text{ matches the pattern}\,\}$

Predicate: $P(w)=\texttt{fullmatch}(\text{pattern}, w)$

Mask: <span class="rule">df['drink'].str.fullmatch(pattern)</span>

\

A filter with <span class="rule">str.contains(pattern)</span> is a membership test too, for a
bigger language: $\Sigma^* L\, \Sigma^*$, the strings that have a part in $L$.

You’ve been doing language membership tests all class, with filters.


## Two views on Regular Expressions {.smaller}

| Meaning  | In Python/Pandas | Anchors |
|---|---|---|
| Full-string match (language) | `re.fullmatch(r'bb+|c[ac]*', s)`<br>`df['col'].str.fullmatch(r'bb+|c[ac]*')` | not needed: the whole string has to fit |
| Substring search (filter) | `re.search(r'bb+|c[ac]*', s)`<br>`df['col'].str.contains(r'bb+|c[ac]*')` | add `^(...)$` to make it a full-string test |

\

Careful: if a pattern matches the empty string, every string has a part that fits.
`df['drink'].str.contains(r'b?')` keeps all 20 café orders.
